I. $\text{curl}\,F=0$

II. $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$

III. $F$ is not irrotational

IV. $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction." :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

![](images/b1/b1520791fcb3808604758b7d8f99443020d12075d4cc8bff78659880575b6ef2.png)

Moreover, if $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statement II is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would not rotate. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- Statements III and IV are false. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational. And, since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ it points in neither the positive nor the negative $z$-direction.

:question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x+2y) \\  & =-2x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(-2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(-2,1)} & =-2(-2)-2 \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-aedf76f0-5451-58bc-9366-057502daac94" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9999ac46-6f4e-593f-907b-51eaf6bed9c7" :answer-field/id #uuid Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- **III.** $F$ is irrotational
- **IV.** $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction." :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

![](images/97/979b63f21e56924bd7880f9487cf829089e38cf14d287e70196c7a661e41f97f.png)

Moreover, if $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statement II is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would not rotate. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- Statement III is true. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational.

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ it points in neither the positive nor the negative $z$-direction.

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

"Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

$$\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$$

If the first partial derivatives of $P, Q,$ and $R$ all exist, then the **curl** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F,$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ given by

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \left(\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \right)\,\mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right)\,\mathbf k.$$

The formula above is pretty tough to remember. Luckily, there is an easier way. If we define the differential operator $\nabla$ (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as

$$\nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}$$

then the curl of $\mathbf F$ is given by the cross product

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F.$$

Expressing the quantity on the right-hand side as a determinant, we have

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F = \left| \begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned} \right|.$$

For example, suppose that the vector field $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=xz\,\mathbf{i}+ xy\,\mathbf{j}+yz\,\mathbf{k}.$$

Then we can calculate $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}$ using the determinant formula as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ xz & xy & yz\end{aligned}| \\ & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz)]k \\ & =(z-0)\,i-(0-x)\,j+(y-0)\,k \\ & =z\,i+x\,j+y\,k\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid 17592186135115 :tutorial/content "We know how to compute the curl of a vector field. Our goal now is to develop an intuitive understanding of what the curl of a vector field measures.

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ shown below. Assume that $\mathbf F$ is independent of $z.$ 

![](images/13/13db0656977bb206ccca66fd25fee08ee2b3c8724173b74aeb4e856109ce0be5.png)

It's helpful to imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. 

Now, we pick an arbitrary point in the $xy$-plane and place a paddlewheel at our point with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction (the direction of the curl).

![](images/0e/0eb70168474799d1b94311f444aef72e1904b0c8e13042ba1ba182cd23e57dba.png)

The curl of the vector field at our point measures how much the paddlewheel rotates due to the action of the water. There are two possible cases, illustrated below.

![](images/86/86aee33cdfa96ac0a61468cc9657e791e399f31c024cdbc3a932193dc897d534.png)

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl. In other words, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq  \mathbf 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F =  \mathbf 0.$ In this case, we say that $\mathbf F$ is **irrotational**.

For the particular point we've chosen in our example, we can see that the action of the water will cause the paddleboard to rotate counterclockwise.

![](images/96/96bfb9c08d2d5ea0c119e8e4ee6a54e8aaa9fee0eabe8fb13b7c65cc586c3094.png)

Since the water causes the paddleboard to rotate, we must have $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0.$

Finally, note that if $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F =\mathbf 0,$ then it does not point in any particular direction." :tutorial/id #uuid "b69ffb3c-f0ed-59d1-b022-ccb162de3d67" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5519 :tutorial/title "Physical Interpretation of the Curl"} :step/id #uuid "b31fa9fe-8595-5f98-bdde-8a55d53eccb1" :step/math-academy-id 34360 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134846}} {:db/id 17592186134845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135117 :tutorial/content "We can only compute the curl of a *vector* field, and a vector field's curl is also a vector field. So if $\mathbf G = \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F,$ then we have the following map:

$$
\underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf F(x,y,z)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}} \mapsto\underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf G(x,y,z)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}}
$$

In contrast, if $f(x,y, z)$ is a scalar field, then the statement $\textrm{curl}\, f$ has no meaning.

The curl of a vector field at a point $P$ gives us helpful information about the rotational behavior of the vector field at $P.$ We'll describe this in more detail shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5a7bd6a-0498-53af-afe7-1a9974db120d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5789 :tutorial/title "Some Notes About the Curl of a Vector Field"} :step/id #uuid "a02eaa37-2a1d-55e1-98e9-5eda118d61d2" :step/math-academy-id 35528 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134823}} {:db/id 17592186134846 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135118 :tutorial/content "In general, when we compute the curl of a vector field at a point, the result is a vector. This vector gives us two pieces of information about the rotation of a paddleboard placed at that point:

- The magnitude of the curl vector indicates the speed of the rotation of the paddleboard.

- The direction of the curl vector gives us the *axis of rotation* on which the paddlewheel should be placed for maximum rotation.

The orientation of the curl vector is determined by the so-called **right-hand rule**. To understand this, let's return to our example:

![](images/96/96bfb9c08d2d5ea0c119e8e4ee6a54e8aaa9fee0eabe8fb13b7c65cc586c3094.png)

Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point *away* from the screen. Therefore, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ also points away from the screen, in the direction of increasing $z.$ 

The situation is reversed when the rotation of the vector field is clockwise:

![](images/4b/4b13f2a96f05124184ad8b7f2007b2267a55679b55e5ed6344a2609696abe0be.png)

Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (clockwise), our thumb will point *into* the screen. Therefore, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ also points into from the screen, in the direction of decreasing $z.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4456c748-e7a9-5576-b733-c6033799f9f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5790 :tutorial/title "The Right-Hand Rule"} :step/id #uuid "7edf68a9-c5bd-5bbc-82e9-a0291639597e" :step/math-academy-id 35529 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134847}} {:db/id 17592186134847 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135119 :tutorial/content "The following two vector fields would both cause a paddleboard to rotate counterclockwise. Therefore, their curl is nonzero.

![](images/92/92654626dae292c06a227622c6eb590df6e7c898eebe1c06d2b3cd57630dfea0.png)

The following two vector fields would both cause a paddleboard to rotate clockwise. Therefore, their curl is nonzero.

![](images/2c/2cda9e8468dff1fdfe3d60c4069054f1f85ea4c6356075b576f69228def7496c.png)

However, it's sometimes helpful to avoid this issue by considering $\mathbf F$ as a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ whose $\mathbf k$ component is zero everywhere. 

Assuming that the $\mathbf k$ component of $\mathbf F$ is zero everywhere, the curl must point in the $z$-direction perpendicular to your screen. To see why, note that if we start from

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k,
$$

then set 

$$
R(x,y,z) = 0, \qquad \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial z}= \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial z} = 0
$$

and, finally, substitute the above into our curl formula, then we get

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F 
= 
\left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right)\,\mathbf k.
$$

Note that the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}
$$

 
is called the **scalar curl** of $\mathbf F.$ The scalar curl is associated with two-dimensional vector fields only." :tutorial/id #uuid "07a27175-fb76-5663-98dd-203ead020fc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5848 :tutorial/title "The Curl of a Two-Dimensional Vector Field"} :step/id #uuid "2f58e72d-0cd5-5224-8856-908ecd564b96" :step/math-academy-id 35822 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134869}}] :activity/title "The Curl of a Vector Field" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134011} {:db/id 17592186134812 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135103 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \left(\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \right)\,\mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right)\,\mathbf k.$$

$$\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$$

If the first partial derivatives of $P, Q,$ and $R$ all exist, then the **curl** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F,$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ given by

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \left(\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \right)\,\mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right)\,\mathbf k.$$

The formula above is pretty tough to remember. Luckily, there is an easier way. If we define the differential operator $\nabla$ (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as

$$\nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}$$

then the curl of $\mathbf F$ is given by the cross product

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F.$$

Expressing the quantity on the right-hand side as a determinant, we have

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F = \left| \begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned} \right|.$$

For example, suppose that the vector field $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=xz\,\mathbf{i}+ xy\,\mathbf{j}+yz\,\mathbf{k}.$$

Then we can calculate $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}$ using the determinant formula as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ xz & xy & yz\end{aligned}| \\ & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz)]k \\ & =(z-0)\,i-(0-x)\,j+(y-0)\,k \\ & =z\,i+x\,j+y\,k\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "748e0ff5-caab-5725-a53e-a87f3322d0b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5141 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186134845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135117 :tutorial/content "We can only compute the curl of a *vector* field, and a vector field's curl is also a vector field. ![](images/13/13db0656977bb206ccca66fd25fee08ee2b3c8724173b74aeb4e856109ce0be5.png)

It's helpful to imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. 

Now, we pick an arbitrary point in the $xy$-plane and place a paddlewheel at our point with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction (the direction of the curl).

![](images/0e/0eb70168474799d1b94311f444aef72e1904b0c8e13042ba1ba182cd23e57dba.png)

For the particular point we've chosen in our example, we can see that the action of the water will cause the paddleboard to rotate counterclockwise.

![](images/96/96bfb9c08d2d5ea0c119e8e4ee6a54e8aaa9fee0eabe8fb13b7c65cc586c3094.png)

Since the water causes the paddleboard to rotate, we must have $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0.$

"![](images/17/17637e938a25e91b9a03921dbbe0f22c8ea760f09cfed9b4a76d07bd5e3b9301.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- **II.** $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- **III.** $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction.
- **IV.** $F$ is irrotational" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/f3/f385add60afac473a5734f8c1ed57c6575bada03c9c16b24fed73b200c38e2c5.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statement I is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement III is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (clockwise), our thumb will point into the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points into the screen, in the direction of decreasing $z.$

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

If the first partial derivatives of $P, Q,$ and $R$ all exist, then the **curl** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F,$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ given by

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \left(\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \right)\,\mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right)\,\mathbf k.$$

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F.$$
